entries.966729a88f6e6fb22208546bff54fec5add9db67: <div sID="gen11021" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="37" osisID="Ps.37" sID="Ps.37"/> <div eID="gen11021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11022" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11023" type="x-p"/> This psalm is a sermon, and an excellent useful sermon it is, calculated not (as most of the psalms) for our devotion, but for our conversation; there is nothing in it of prayer or praise, but it is all instruction; it is "Maschil—a teaching psalm;" it is an exposition of some of the hardest chapters in the book of Providence, the advancement of the wicked and the disgrace of the righteous, a solution of the difficulties that arise thereupon, and an exhortation to conduct ourselves as becomes us under such dark dispensations. The work of the prophets (and David was one) was to explain the law. Now the law of Moses had promised temporal blessings to the obedient, and denounced temporal miseries against the disobedient, which principally referred to the body of the people, the nation as a nation; for, when they came to be applied to particular persons, many instances occurred of sinners in prosperity and saints in adversity; to reconcile those instances with the word that God had spoken is the scope of the prophet in this psalm, in which, I. He forbids us to fret at the prosperity of the wicked in their wicked ways, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.7">7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.8">8</reference>. II. He gives very good reasons why we should not fret at it. 1. Because of the scandalous character of the wicked (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.12">ver. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.14">14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.21">21,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.32">32</reference>) notwithstanding their prosperity, and the honourable character of the righteous, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.21">ver. 21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.26">26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.30">30,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.31">31</reference>. 2. Because of the destruction and ruin which the wicked are nigh to (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.2 Ps.37.9 Ps.37.10 Ps.37.20 Ps.37.35 Ps.37.36 Ps.37.38">ver. 2, 9, 10, 20, 35, 36, 38</reference>) and the salvation and protection which the righteous are sure of from all the malicious designs of the wicked, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.13 Ps.37.15 Ps.37.17 Ps.37.28 Ps.37.33 Ps.37.39 Ps.37.40">ver. 13, 15, 17, 28, 33, 39, 40</reference>. 3. Because of the particular mercy God has in store for all good people and the favour he shows them, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.11 Ps.37.16 Ps.37.18 Ps.37.19 Ps.37.22-Ps.37.25 Ps.37.28 Ps.37.29 Ps.37.37">ver. 11, 16, 18, 19, 22-25, 28, 29, 37</reference>. III. He prescribes very good remedies against this sin of envying the prosperity of the wicked, and great encouragement to use those remedies, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.3-Ps.37.6">ver. 3-6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.27">27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.34">34</reference>. In singing this psalm we must teach and admonish one another rightly to understand the providence of God and to accommodate ourselves to it, at all times carefully to do our duty and then patiently to leave the event with God and to believe that, how black soever things may look for the present, it shall be "well with those that fear God, that fear before him."
entries.d565e7ecb60334c73052cf08acc112c7150fb9c2: <div eID="gen11023" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11022" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Exhortations and Promises.</title> <div sID="gen11024" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity. <hi type="super">2</hi> For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb. <hi type="super">3</hi> Trust in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and do good; <hi type="italic">so</hi> shalt thou dwell in the land, and verily thou shalt be fed. <hi type="super">4</hi> Delight thyself also in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart. <hi type="super">5</hi> Commit thy way unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; trust also in him; and he shall bring <hi type="italic">it</hi> to pass. <hi type="super">6</hi> And he shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday. <div eID="gen11024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11025" type="x-p"/> The instructions here given are very plain; much need not be said for the exposition of them, but there is a great deal to be done for the reducing of them to practice, and there they will look best. <div eID="gen11025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11026" type="x-p"/> I. We are here cautioned against discontent at the prosperity and success of evil-doers (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.1-Ps.37.2">v. 1, 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Fret not thyself, neither be thou envious.</hi> We may suppose that David speaks this to himself first, and preaches it to his own heart (in his communing with that upon his bed), for the suppressing of those corrupt passions which he found working there, and then leaves it in writing for instruction to others that might be in similar temptation. That is preached best, and with most probability of success, to others, which is first preached to ourselves. Now, 1. When we look abroad we see the world full of evil-doers and workers of iniquity, that flourish and prosper, that have what they will and do what they will, that live in ease and pomp themselves and have power in their hands to do mischief to those about them. So it was in David's time; and therefore, if it is so still, let us not marvel at the matter, as though it were some new or strange thing. 2. When we look within we find ourselves tempted to fret at this, and to be envious against these scandals and burdens, these blemishes and common nuisances, of this earth. We are apt to fret at God, as if he were unkind to the world and unkind to his church in permitting such men to live, and prosper, and prevail, as they do. We are apt to fret ourselves with vexation at their success in their evil projects. We are apt to envy them the liberty they take in getting wealth, and perhaps by unlawful means, and in the indulgence of their lusts, and to wish that we could shake off the restraints of conscience and do so too. We are tempted to think them the only happy people, and to incline to imitate them, and to join ourselves with them, that we may share in their gains and eat of their dainties; and this is that which we are warned against: <hi type="italic">Fret not thyself, neither be thou envious.</hi> Fretfulness and envy are sins that are their own punishments; they are the uneasiness of the spirit and the rottenness of the bones; it is therefore in kindness to ourselves that we are warned against them. Yet that is not all; for, 3. When we look forward with an eye of faith we shall see no reason to envy wicked people their prosperity, for their ruin is at the door and they are ripening apace for it, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.2">v. 2</reference>. They flourish, but as the grass, and as the green herb, which nobody envies nor frets at. The flourishing of a godly man is like that of a fruitful tree (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.3">Ps. i. 3</reference>), but that of the wicked man is like grass and herbs, which are very short-lived. (1.) They will soon wither of themselves. Outward prosperity is a fading thing, and so is the life itself to which it is confined. (2.) They will sooner be cut down by the judgments of God. Their triumphing is short, but their weeping and wailing will be everlasting. <div eID="gen11026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11027" type="x-p"/> II. We are here counselled to live a life on confidence and complacency in God, and that will keep us from fretting at the prosperity of evil-doers; if we do well for our own souls, we shall see little reason to envy those that do so ill for theirs. Here are three excellent precepts, which we are to be ruled by, and, to enforce them, three precious promises, which we may rely upon. <div eID="gen11027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11028" type="x-p"/> 1. We must make God our hope in the way of duty and then we shall have a comfortable subsistence in this world, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.3">v. 3</reference>. (1.) It is required that we <hi type="italic">trust in the Lord and do good,</hi> that we confide in God and conform to him. The life of religion lies much in a believing reliance on God, his favour, his providence, his promise, his grace, and a diligent care to serve him and our generation, according to his will. We must not think to trust in God and then live as we wish. No; it is not trusting God, but tempting him, if we do not make conscience of our duty to him. Nor must we think to do good, and then to trust to ourselves, and our own righteousness and strength. No; we must both trust in the Lord and do good. And then, (2.) It is promised that we shall be well provided for in this world: <hi type="italic">So shalt thou dwell in the land, and verily thou shalt be fed.</hi> He does not say, "So shalt thou get preferment, dwell in a palace, and be feasted." This is not necessary; a man's life consists not in the abundance of these things; but, "Thou shalt have a place to live in, and that in the land, in Canaan, the valley of vision, and thou shalt have food convenient for thee." This is more than we deserve; it is as much as a good man will stipulate for (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.20">Gen. xxviii. 20</reference>) and it is enough for one that is going to heaven. "Thou shalt have a settlement, a quiet settlement, and a maintenance, a comfortable maintenance: <hi type="italic">Verily thou shalt be fed.</hi>" Some read it, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be fed by faith,</hi> as the just are said to live by faith, and it is good living, good feeding, upon the promises. "<hi type="italic">Verily thou shalt be fed,</hi> as Elijah in the famine, with what is needful for thee." God himself is a shepherd, a feeder, to all those that trust in him, <reference osisRef="Ps.23.1">Ps. xxiii. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen11028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11029" type="x-p"/> 2. We must make God our heart's delight and then we shall have our heart's desire, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.4">v. 4</reference>. We must not only depend upon God, but solace ourselves in him. We must be well pleased that there is a God, that he is such a one as he has revealed himself to be, and that he is our God in covenant. We must delight ourselves in his beauty, bounty, and benignity; our souls must return to him, and repose in him, as their rest, and their portion for ever. Being satisfied of his loving-kindness, we must be satisfied with it, and make that our exceeding joy, <reference osisRef="Ps.43.4">Ps. xliii. 4</reference>. We were commanded (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.3">v. 3</reference>) to do good, and then follows this command to delight in God, which is as much a privilege as a duty. If we make conscience of obedience to God, we may then take the comfort of a complacency in him. And even this pleasant duty of delighting in God has a promise annexed to it, which is very full and precious, enough to recompense the hardest services: <hi type="italic">He shall give thee the desires of thy heart.</hi> He has not promised to gratify all the appetites of the body and the humours of the fancy, but to grant all the desires of the heart, all the cravings of the renewed sanctified soul. What is the desire of the heart of a good man? It is this, to know, and love, and live to God, to please him and to be pleased in him. <div eID="gen11029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11030" type="x-p"/> 3. We must make God our guide, and submit in every thing to his guidance and disposal; and then all our affairs, even those that seem most intricate and perplexed, shall be made to issue well and to our satisfaction, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.5-Ps.37.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. (1.) The duty is very easy; and, if we do it aright, it will make us easy: <hi type="italic">Commit thy way unto the Lord; roll thy way upon the Lord</hi> (so the margin reads it), <reference osisRef="Prov.16.3">Prov. xvi. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.22">Ps. lv. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">Cast thy burden upon the Lord,</hi> the burden of thy care, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.7">1 Pet. v. 7</reference>. We must roll it off ourselves, so as not to afflict and perplex ourselves with thoughts about future events (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.25">Matt. vi. 25</reference>), not to cumber and trouble ourselves either with the contrivance of the means or with expectation of the end, but refer it to God, leave it to him by his wise and good providence to order and dispose of all our concerns as he pleases. <hi type="italic">Retreat thy way unto the Lord</hi> (so the LXX.), that is, "By prayer spread thy case, and all thy cares about it, before the Lord" (as Jephthah <hi type="italic">uttered all his words before the Lord in Mizpeh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.11.11">Judg. xi. 11</reference>), "and then trust in him to bring it to a good issue, with a full satisfaction that all is well that God does." We must do our duty (that must be our care) and then leave the event with God. <hi type="italic">Sit still, and see how the matter will fall,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ruth.3.18">Ruth iii. 18</reference>. We must follow Providence, and not force it, subscribe to Infinite Wisdom and not prescribe. (2.) The promise is very sweet. [1.] In general, "<hi type="italic">He shall bring that to pass,</hi> whatever it is, which thou hast committed to him, if not to thy contrivance, yet to thy content. He will find means to extricate thee out of thy straits, to prevent thy fears, and bring about thy purposes, to thy satisfaction." [2.] In particular, "He will take care of thy reputation, and bring thee out of thy difficulties, not only with comfort, but with credit and honour: <hi type="italic">He shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light and thy judgment as the noon-day.</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.6">v. 6</reference>), that is, "he shall make it to appear that thou art an honest man, and that is honour enough." <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is implied that the righteousness and judgment of good people may, for a time, be clouded and eclipsed, either by remarkable rebukes of Providence (Job's great afflictions darkened his righteousness) or by the malicious censures and reproaches of men, who give them bad names which they no way deserve, and lay to their charge things which they know not. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is promised that God will, in due time, roll away the reproach they are under, clear up their innocency, and bring forth their righteousness, to their honour, perhaps in this world, at furthest in the great day, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.43">Matt. xiii. 43</reference>. Note, If we take care to keep a good conscience, we may leave it to God to take care of our good name.
entries.e975e50316d55b83e06bff4f9dd41600dc227d34: <div eID="gen11030" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Exhortations and Promises.</title> <div sID="gen11031" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Rest in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass. <hi type="super">8</hi> Cease from anger, and forsake wrath: fret not thyself in any wise to do evil. <hi type="super">9</hi> For evildoers shall be cut off: but those that wait upon the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , they shall inherit the earth. 10 For yet a little while, and the wicked <hi type="italic">shall</hi> not <hi type="italic">be:</hi> yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it <hi type="italic">shall</hi> not <hi type="italic">be.</hi> <hi type="super">11</hi> But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace. 12 The wicked plotteth against the just, and gnasheth upon him with his teeth. <hi type="super">13</hi> The Lord shall laugh at him: for he seeth that his day is coming. <hi type="super">14</hi> The wicked have drawn out the sword, and have bent their bow, to cast down the poor and needy, <hi type="italic">and</hi> to slay such as be of upright conversation. 15 Their sword shall enter into their own heart, and their bows shall be broken. <hi type="super">16</hi> A little that a righteous man hath <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than the riches of many wicked. <hi type="super">17</hi> For the arms of the wicked shall be broken: but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> upholdeth the righteous. <hi type="super">18</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> knoweth the days of the upright: and their inheritance shall be for ever. <hi type="super">19</hi> They shall not be ashamed in the evil time: and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied. <hi type="super">20</hi> But the wicked shall perish, and the enemies of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> as the fat of lambs: they shall consume; into smoke shall they consume away. <div eID="gen11031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11032" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen11032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11033" type="x-p"/> I. The foregoing precepts inculcated; for we are so apt to disquiet ourselves with needless fruitless discontents and distrusts that it is necessary there should be precept upon precept, and line upon line, to suppress them and arm us against them. 1. Let us compose ourselves by believing in God: "<hi type="italic">Rest in the Lord, and wait patiently for him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.7">v. 7</reference>), that is, be well reconciled to all he does and acquiesce in it, for that is best that is, because it is what God has appointed; and be well satisfied that he will still make all to work for good to us, though we know not how or which way." <hi type="italic">Be silent to the Lord</hi> (so the word is), not with a sullen, but a submissive silence. A patient bearing of what is laid upon us, with a patient expectation of what is further appointed for us, is as much our interest as it is our duty, for it will make us always easy; and there is a great deal of reason for it, for it is making a virtue of necessity. 2. Let us not discompose ourselves at what we see in this world: "<hi type="italic">Fret not thyself because of him who prospers in his wicked way,</hi> who, though he is a bad man, yet thrives and grows rich and great in the world; no, nor because of him who does mischief with his power and wealth, and brings wicked devices to pass against those that are virtuous and good, who seems to have gained his point and to have run them down. If thy heart begins to rise at it, stroke down thy folly, and <hi type="italic">cease from anger</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.8">v. 8</reference>), check the first stirrings of discontent and envy, and do not harbour any hard thoughts of God and his providence upon this account. Be not angry at any thing that God does, but forsake that wrath; it is the worst kind of wrath that can be. <hi type="italic">Fret not thyself in any wise to do evil;</hi> do not envy them their prosperity, lest thou be tempted to fall in with them and to take the same evil course that they take to enrich and advance themselves or some desperate course to avoid them and their power." Note, A fretful discontented spirit lies open to many temptations; and those that indulge it are in danger of doing evil. <div eID="gen11033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11034" type="x-p"/> II. The foregoing reasons, taken from the approaching ruin of the wicked notwithstanding their prosperity, and the real happiness of the righteous notwithstanding their troubles, are here much enlarged upon and the same things repeated in a pleasing variety of expression. We were cautioned (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.7">v. 7</reference>) not to envy the wicked either worldly prosperity or the success of their plots against the righteous, and the reasons here given respect these two temptations severally:— <div eID="gen11034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11035" type="x-p"/> 1. Good people have no reason to envy the worldly prosperity of wicked people, nor to grieve or be uneasy at it, (1.) Because the prosperity of the wicked will soon be at an end (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Evil-doers shall be cut off</hi> by some sudden stroke of divine justice in the midst of their prosperity; what they have got by sin will not only flow away from them (<reference osisRef="Job.20.28">Job xx. 28</reference>), but they shall be carried away with it. See the end of these men (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">Ps. lxxiii. 17</reference>), how dear their ill-got gain will cost them, and you will be far from envying them or from being willing to espouse their lot, for better, for worse. Their ruin is sure, and it is very near (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be</hi> what they now are; <hi type="italic">they are brought into desolation in a moment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.19">Ps. lxxiii. 19</reference>. Have a little patience, for <hi type="italic">the Judge stands before the door,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.5.8-Jas.5.9">Jam. v. 8, 9</reference>. Moderate your passion, <hi type="italic">for the Lord is at hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.5">Phil. iv. 5</reference>. And when their ruin comes it will be an utter ruin; he and his shall be extirpated; the day that comes shall <hi type="italic">leave him neither root nor branch</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.4.1">Mal. iv. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt diligently consider his place,</hi> where but the other day he made a mighty figure, but <hi type="italic">it shall not be,</hi> you will not find it; he shall leave nothing valuable, nothing honourable, behind. him. To the same purport (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.20">v. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">The wicked shall perish;</hi> their death is their perdition, because it is the termination of all their joy and a passage to endless misery. <hi type="italic">Blessed are the dead that die in the Lord;</hi> but undone, for ever undone, are the dead that die in their sins. The wicked are the enemies of the Lord; such those make themselves who will not have him to reign over them, and as such he will reckon with them: <hi type="italic">They shall consume as the fat of lambs, they shall consume into smoke.</hi> Their prosperity, which gratifies their sensuality, is like the fat of lambs, not solid or substantial, but loose and washy; and, when their ruin comes, they shall fall as sacrifices to the justice of God and be consumed as the fat of the sacrifices was upon the altar, whence it ascended in smoke. The day of God's vengeance on the wicked is represented as a <hi type="italic">sacrifice of the fat of the kidneys of rams</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.6">Isa. xxxiv. 6</reference>); for he will be honoured by the ruin of his enemies, as he was by the sacrifices. Damned sinners are sacrifices, <reference osisRef="Mark.9.49">Mark ix. 49</reference>. This is a good reason why we should not envy them their prosperity; while they are fed to the full, they are but in the fattening for the day of sacrifice, <hi type="italic">like a lamb in a large place</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.16">Hos. iv. 16</reference>), and the more they prosper the more will God be glorified in their ruin. (2.) Because the condition of the righteous, even in this life, is every way better and more desirable than that of the wicked, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.16">v. 16</reference>. In general, <hi type="italic">a little that a righteous man has</hi> of the honour, wealth, and pleasure of this world, <hi type="italic">is better than the riches of many wicked.</hi> Observe, [1.] The wealth of the world is so dispensed by the divine Providence that it is often the lot of good people to have but a little of it, and of wicked people to have abundance of it; for thus God would show us that the things of this world are not the best things, for, if they were, those would have most that are best and dearest to God. [2.] That a godly man's little is really better than a wicked man's estate, though ever so much; for it comes from a better hand, from a hand of special love and not merely from a hand of common providence,—it is enjoyed by a better title (God gives it to them by promise, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.18">Gal. iii. 18</reference>),—it is theirs by virtue of their relation to Christ, who is the heir of all things,—and it is put to better use; it is sanctified to them by the blessing of God. <hi type="italic">Unto the pure all things are pure,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit. i. 15</reference>. A little wherewith God is served and honoured is better than a great deal prepared for Baal or for a base lust. The promises here made to the righteous secure them such a happiness that they need not envy the prosperity of evil-doers. Let them know to their comfort, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That <hi type="italic">they shall inherit the earth,</hi> as much of it as Infinite Wisdom sees good for them; they have the promise of the <hi type="italic">life that now is,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.8">1 Tim. iv. 8</reference>. If all the earth were necessary to make them happy, they should have it. All is theirs, even <hi type="italic">the world,</hi> and <hi type="italic">things present,</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">things to come,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.21-1Cor.3.22">1 Cor. iii. 21, 22</reference>. They have it by inheritance, a safe and honourable title, not by permission only and connivance. When evil-doers are cut off the righteous sometimes inherit what they gathered. <hi type="italic">The wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.27.17">Job xxvii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.13.22">Prov. xiii. 22</reference>. This promise is here made, 1. To those that live a life of faith (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.9">v. 9</reference>); <hi type="italic">Those that wait upon the Lord,</hi> as dependents on him, expectants from him, and suppliants to him, <hi type="italic">shall inherit the earth,</hi> as a token of his present favour to them and an earnest of better things intended for them in the other world. God is a good Master, that provides plentifully and well, not only for his working servants, but for his waiting servants. 2. To those that live a quiet and peaceable life (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The meek shall inherit the earth.</hi> They are in least danger of being injured and disturbed in the possession of what they have and they have most satisfaction in themselves and consequently the sweetest relish of their creature-comforts. Our Saviour has made this a gospel promise, and a confirmation of the blessings he pronounced on the meek, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.5">Matt. v. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That they <hi type="italic">shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.11">v. 11</reference>. Perhaps they have not abundance of wealth to delight in; but they have that which is better, abundance of peace, inward peace and tranquility of mind, peace with God, and then peace in God, that great peace which those have that love God's law, whom <hi type="italic">nothing shall offend</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.165">Ps. cxix. 165</reference>), that abundance of peace which is in the kingdom of Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.7">Ps. lxxii. 7</reference>), that peace which the world cannot give (<reference osisRef="John.14.27">John xiv. 27</reference>), and which the wicked cannot have, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.21">Isa. lvii. 21</reference>. This they shall delight themselves in, and in it they shall have a continual feast; while those that have abundance of wealth do but cumber and perplex themselves with it and have little delight in it. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That God <hi type="italic">knows their days,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.18">v. 18</reference>. He takes particular notice of them, of all they do and of all that happens to them. He keeps account of the days of their service, and not one day's work shall go unrewarded, and of the days of their suffering, that for those also they may receive a recompence. He knows their bright days, and has pleasure in their prosperity; he knows their cloudy and dark days, the days of their affliction, and as the day is so shall the strength be. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> That <hi type="italic">their inheritance shall be for ever;</hi> not their inheritance in the earth, but that incorruptible indefeasible one which is laid up for them in heaven. Those that are sure of an everlasting inheritance in the other world have no reason to envy the wicked their transitory possessions and pleasures in this world. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> That in the worst of times it shall go well with them (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall not be ashamed</hi> of their hope and confidence in God, nor of the profession they have made of religion; for the comfort of that will stand them in stead, and be a real support to them, in evil times. When others droop they shall lift up their heads with joy and confidence: Even <hi type="italic">in the days of famine,</hi> when others are dying for hunger round about them, <hi type="italic">they shall be satisfied,</hi> as Elijah was; in some way or other God will provide food convenient for them, or give them hearts to be satisfied and content without it, so that, if they should be hardly bestead and hungry, they shall not (as the wicked do) <hi type="italic">fret themselves and curse their king and their God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.21">Isa. vii. 21</reference>), but rejoice in God as the God of their salvation even when <hi type="italic">the fig-tree does not blossom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.3.17-Hab.3.18">Hab. iii. 17, 18</reference>. <div eID="gen11035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11036" type="x-p"/> 2. Good people have no reason to fret at the occasional success of the designs of the wicked against the just. Though they do bring some of their wicked devices to pass, which makes us fear they will gain their point and bring them all to pass, yet let us cease from anger, and not fret ourselves so as to think of giving up the cause. For, <div eID="gen11036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11037" type="x-p"/> (1.) Their plots will be their shame, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.12-Ps.37.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. It is true <hi type="italic">the wicked plotteth against the just;</hi> there is a rooted enmity in the seed of the wicked one against the righteous seed; their aim is, if they can, to destroy their righteousness, or, if that fail, then to destroy them. With this end in view they have acted with a great deal both of cursed policy and contrivance (they plot, they practice, against the just), and of cursed zeal and fury—<hi type="italic">they gnash upon them with their teeth,</hi> so desirous are they, if they could get it into their power, to eat them up, and so full of rage and indignation are they because it is not in their power; but by all this they do but make themselves ridiculous. <hi type="italic">The Lord shall laugh at them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.4-Ps.2.5">Ps. ii. 4, 5</reference>. They are proud and insolent, but God shall pour contempt upon them. He is not only displeased with them, but he despises them and all their attempts as vain and ineffectual, and their malice as impotent and in a chain; <hi type="italic">for he sees that his day is coming,</hi> that is, [1.] The day of God's reckoning, the day of the revelation of his righteousness, which now seems clouded and eclipsed. Men have their day now. <hi type="italic">This is your hour,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.22.53">Luke xxii. 53</reference>. But God will have his day shortly, a day of recompences, a day which will set all to rights, and render that ridiculous which now passes for glorious. <hi type="italic">It is a small thing to be judged of man's judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.3">1 Cor. iv. 3</reference>. God's day will give a decisive judgment. [2.] The day of their ruin. The wicked man's day, the day set for his fall, that day <hi type="italic">is coming,</hi> which denotes delay; it has not yet come, but certainly it will come. The believing prospect of that day will enable the virgin, the daughter of Zion, to despise the rage of her enemies and <hi type="italic">laugh them to scorn,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.37.22">Isa. xxxvii. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen11037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11038" type="x-p"/> (2.) Their attempts will be their destruction, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.14-Ps.37.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. See here, [1.] How cruel they are in their designs against good people. They prepare instruments of death, <hi type="italic">the sword</hi> and <hi type="italic">the bow,</hi> no less will serve; they hunt for the precious life. That which they design is <hi type="italic">to cast down and slay;</hi> it is the blood of the saints they thirst after. They carry on the design very far, and it is near to be put in execution: They <hi type="italic">have drawn the sword, and bent the bow;</hi> and all these military preparations are made against the helpless, <hi type="italic">the poor and needy</hi> (which proves them to be very cowardly), and against the guiltless, <hi type="italic">such as are of upright conversation,</hi> that never gave them any provocation, nor offered injury to them or any other person, which proves them to be very wicked. Uprightness itself will be no fence against their malice. But, [2.] How justly their malice recoils upon themselves: <hi type="italic">Their sword shall turn into their own heart,</hi> which implies the preservation of the righteous from their malice and the filling up of the measure of their own iniquity by it. Sometimes that very thing proves to be their own destruction which they projected against their harmless neighbours; however, God's sword, which their provocations have drawn against them, will give them their death's wound. <div eID="gen11038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11039" type="x-p"/> (3.) Those that are not suddenly cut off shall yet be so disabled for doing any further mischief that the interests of the church shall be effectually secured: <hi type="italic">Their bows shall be broken</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.15">v. 15</reference>); the instruments of their cruelty shall fail them and they shall lose those whom they had made tools of to serve their bloody purposes with; nay, <hi type="italic">their arms shall be broken,</hi> so that they shall not be able to go on with their enterprises, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.17">v. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">But the Lord upholds the righteous,</hi> so that they neither sink under the weight of their afflictions nor are crushed by the violence of their enemies. He upholds them both in their integrity and in their prosperity; and those that are so upheld by the rock of ages have no reason to envy the wicked the support of their broken reeds.
entries.00f9175f2888fa8869330a0eed072ef9824a8672: <div eID="gen11039" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Exhortations and Promises.</title> <div sID="gen11040" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous showeth mercy, and giveth. <hi type="super">22</hi> For <hi type="italic">such as be</hi> blessed of him shall inherit the earth; and <hi type="italic">they that be</hi> cursed of him shall be cut off. <hi type="super">23</hi> The steps of a <hi type="italic">good</hi> man are ordered by the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and he delighteth in his way. <hi type="super">24</hi> Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> upholdeth <hi type="italic">him with</hi> his hand. 25 I have been young, and <hi type="italic">now</hi> am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread. 26 <hi type="italic">He is</hi> ever merciful, and lendeth; and his seed <hi type="italic">is</hi> blessed. <hi type="super">27</hi> Depart from evil, and do good; and dwell for evermore. <hi type="super">28</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> loveth judgment, and forsaketh not his saints; they are preserved for ever: but the seed of the wicked shall be cut off. <hi type="super">29</hi> The righteous shall inherit the land, and dwell therein for ever. 30 The mouth of the righteous speaketh wisdom, and his tongue talketh of judgment. <hi type="super">31</hi> The law of his God <hi type="italic">is</hi> in his heart; none of his steps shall slide. <hi type="super">32</hi> The wicked watcheth the righteous, and seeketh to slay him. <hi type="super">33</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will not leave him in his hand, nor condemn him when he is judged. <div eID="gen11040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11041" type="x-p"/> These verses are much to the same purport with the <reference osisRef="Ps.37.1-Ps.37.20">foregoing verses</reference> of this psalm, for it is a subject worthy to be dwelt upon. Observe here, <div eID="gen11041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11042" type="x-p"/> I. What is required of us as the way to our happiness, which we may learn both from the characters here laid down and from the directions here given. If we would be blessed of God, 1. We must make conscience of giving every body his own; for <hi type="italic">the wicked borrows and pays not again,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.21">v. 21</reference>. It is the first thing which the Lord our God requires of us, that we do justly, and render to all their due. It is not only a shameful paltry thing, but a sinful wicked thing, not to repay what we have borrowed. Some make this an instance, not so much of the wickedness of the wicked as of the misery and poverty to which they are reduced by the just judgment of God, that they shall be necessitated to borrow for their supply and then be in no capacity to repay it again, and so lie at the mercy of their creditors. Whatever some men seem to think of it, as it is a great sin for those that are able to deny the payment of their just debts, so it is a great misery not to be able to pay them. 2. We must be ready to all acts of charity and beneficence; for, as it is an instance of God's goodness to the righteous that he puts it into the power of his hand to be kind and to do good (and so some understand it, God's blessing increases his little to such a degree that he has abundance to spare for the relief of others), so it is an instance of the goodness of the righteous man that he has a heart proportionable to his estate: <hi type="italic">He shows mercy, and gives,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.21">v. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">He is ever merciful,</hi> or every day, or all the day, merciful, <hi type="italic">and lends,</hi> and sometimes there is as true charity in lending as in giving; and giving and lending are acceptable to God when they proceed from a merciful disposition in the heart, which, if it be sincere, will be constant, and will keep us from being weary of well-doing. he that is truly merciful will be ever merciful. 3. We must leave our sins, and engage in the practice of serious godliness (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">Depart from evil and do good.</hi> Cease to do evil and abhor it; learn to do well and cleave to it; this is true religion. 4. We must abound in good discourse, and with our tongues must glorify God and edify others. It is part of the character of a righteous man (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.30">v. 30</reference>) that his <hi type="italic">mouth speaketh wisdom;</hi> not only he speaks wisely, but he speaks wisdom, like Solomon himself, for the instruction of those about him. <hi type="italic">His tongue talks</hi> not of things idle and impertinent, but <hi type="italic">of judgment,</hi> that is, of the word and providence of God and the rules of wisdom for the right ordering of the conversation. Out of the abundance of a good heart will the mouth speak that which is good and to the use of edifying. 5. We must have our wills brought into an entire subjection to the will and word of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">The law of God,</hi> of his God, <hi type="italic">is in his heart;</hi> and in vain do we pretend that God is our God if we do not receive his law into our hearts and resign ourselves to the government of it. It is but a jest and a mockery to speak wisdom, and to talk of judgment (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.30">v. 30</reference>), unless we have the law in our hearts, and we think as we speak. The law of God must be a commanding ruling principle in the heart; it must be a light there, a spring there, and then the conversation will be regular and uniform: <hi type="italic">None of his steps will slide;</hi> it will effectually prevent backsliding into sin, and the uneasiness that follows from it. <div eID="gen11042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11043" type="x-p"/> II. What is assured to us, as instances of our happiness and comfort, upon these conditions. <div eID="gen11043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11044" type="x-p"/> 1. That we shall have the blessing of God, and that blessing shall be the spring, and sweetness, and security of all our temporal comforts and enjoyments (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">Such as are blessed of God,</hi> as all the righteous are, with a Father's blessing, by virtue of that <hi type="italic">shall inherit the earth,</hi> or <hi type="italic">the land</hi> (for so the same word is translated, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.29">v. 29</reference>), the land of Canaan, that glory of all lands. Our creature-comforts are comforts indeed to us when we see them flowing from the blessing of God, we are sure not to want any thing that is good for us in this world. <hi type="italic">The earth shall yield us her increase</hi> if God, as <hi type="italic">our own God, give us his blessing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.67.6">Ps. lxvii. 6</reference>. And as <hi type="italic">those whom God blesses are</hi> thus <hi type="italic">blessed indeed (for they shall inherit the land</hi>), so <hi type="italic">those whom he curses are cursed indeed;</hi> they <hi type="italic">shall be cut off</hi> and rooted out, and their extirpation by the divine curse will set off the establishment of the righteous by the divine blessing and be a foil to it. <div eID="gen11044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11045" type="x-p"/> 2. That God will direct and dispose of our actions and affairs so as may be most for his glory (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">The steps of a good man are ordered by the Lord.</hi> By his grace and Holy Spirit he directs the thoughts, affections, and designs of good men. He has all hearts in his hand, but theirs by their own consent. By his providence he overrules the events that concern them, so as to make their way plain before them, both what they should do and what they may expect. Observe, God orders the steps of a good man; not only his way in general, by his written word, but his particular steps, by the whispers of conscience, saying, <hi type="italic">This is the way, walk in it.</hi> He does not always show him his way at a distance, but leads him step by step, as children are led, and so keeps him in a continual dependence upon his guidance; and this, (1.) Because <hi type="italic">he delights in his way,</hi> and is well pleased with the paths of righteousness wherein he walks. <hi type="italic">The Lord knows the way of the righteous</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Ps. i. 6</reference>), knows it with favour, and therefore directs it. (2.) That he may delight in his way. Because God orders his way according to his own will, therefore he delights in it; for, as he loves his own image upon us, so he is well pleased with what we do under his guidance. <div eID="gen11045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11046" type="x-p"/> 3. That God will keep us from being ruined by our falls either into sin or into trouble (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down.</hi> (1.) A good man may be overtaken in a fault, but the grace of God shall recover him to repentance, so that he shall not be utterly cast down. Though he may, for a time, lose the joys of God's salvation, yet they shall be restored to him; for God shall uphold him with his hand, uphold him with his free Spirit. The root shall be kept alive, though the leaf wither; and there will come a spring after the winter. (2.) A good man may be in distress, his affairs embarrassed, his spirits sunk, but he shall not be utterly cast down; God will be the strength of his heart when his flesh and heart fail, and will uphold him with his comforts, so that the spirit he has made shall not fail before him. <div eID="gen11046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11047" type="x-p"/> 4. That we shall not want the necessary supports of this life (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.25">v. 25</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have been young and now am old,</hi> and, among all the changes I have seen in men's outward condition and the observations I have made upon them, <hi type="italic">I never saw the righteous forsaken</hi> of God and man, as I have sometimes seen wicked people abandoned both by heaven and earth; nor do I ever remember to have seen the seed of the righteous reduced to such an extremity as to beg their bread." David had himself begged his bread of Abimelech the priest, but it was when Saul hunted him; and our Saviour has taught us to except the case of persecution for righteousness' sake out of all the temporal promises (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.30">Mark x. 30</reference>), because that has such peculiar honours and comforts attending it as make it rather a gift (as the apostle reckons it, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.29">Phil. i. 29</reference>) than a loss or grievance. But there are very few instances of good men, or their families, that are reduced to such extreme poverty as many wicked people bring themselves to by their wickedness. He had not <hi type="italic">seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging their bread. Forsaken</hi> (so some expound it); if they do want God will raise them up friends to supply them, without a scandalous exposing of themselves to the reproach of common beggars; or, if they go from door to door for meat, it shall not be with despair, as the wicked man <hi type="italic">that wanders abroad for bread, saying, Where is it?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.15.23">Job xv. 23</reference>. Nor shall he be denied, as the prodigal, that <hi type="italic">would fain have filled his belly, but no man gave unto him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.15.16">Luke xv. 16</reference>. Nor shall he grudge if he be not satisfied, as David's enemies, when they <hi type="italic">wandered up and down for meat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.59.15">Ps. lix. 15</reference>. Some make this promise relate especially to those that are charitable and liberal to the poor, and to intimate that David never observed any that brought themselves to poverty by their charity. It is <hi type="italic">withholding more than is meet that tends to poverty,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.24">Prov. xi. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen11047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11048" type="x-p"/> 5. That God will not desert us, but graciously protect us in our difficulties and straits (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord loves judgment;</hi> he delights in doing justice himself and he delights in those that do justice; and therefore he forsakes not his saints in affliction when others make themselves strange to them and become shy of them, but he takes care that they be <hi type="italic">preserved for ever,</hi> that is, that the saint in every age be taken under his protection, that the succession be preserved to the end of time, and that particular saints be preserved from all the temptations and through all the trials of this present time, to that happiness which shall be for ever. He will <hi type="italic">preserve them to his heavenly kingdom;</hi> that is a preservation for ever, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.18">2 Tim. iv. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.12.7">Ps. xii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen11048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11049" type="x-p"/> 6. That we shall have a comfortable settlement in this world, and in a better when we leave this. That we shall <hi type="italic">dwell for evermore</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.27">v. 27</reference>), and not be <hi type="italic">cut off</hi> as the <hi type="italic">seed of the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.28">v. 28</reference>. Those shall not be tossed that make God their rest and are at home in him. But on this earth there is no dwelling for ever, no continuing city; it is in heaven only, that city which has foundations, that the righteous shall dwell for ever; that will be their everlasting habitation. <div eID="gen11049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11050" type="x-p"/> 7. That we shall not become a prey to our adversaries, who seek our ruin, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.32-Ps.37.33">v. 32, 33</reference>. There is an adversary that takes all opportunities to do us a mischief, a wicked one that watches the righteous (as a roaring lion watches his prey) and seeks to slay him. There are wicked men that do so, that are very subtle (they watch the righteous, that they may have an opportunity to do them a mischief effectually and may have a pretence wherewith to justify themselves in the doing of it), and very spiteful, for they seek to slay him. But it may very well be applied to the wicked one, the devil, that old serpent, who has his wiles to entrap the righteous, his devices which we should not be ignorant of,—that great red dragon, who seeks to slay them,—that roaring lion, who goes about continually, restless and raging, and seeking whom he may devour. But it is here promised that he shall not prevail, neither Satan nor his instruments. (1.) He shall not prevail as a field-adversary: <hi type="italic">The Lord will not leave him in his hand;</hi> he will not permit Satan to do what he would, nor will he withdraw his strength and grace from his people, but will enable them to resist and overcome him, and <hi type="italic">their faith shall not fail,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.22.31-Luke.22.32">Luke xxii. 31, 32</reference>. A good man may fall into the hands of a messenger of Satan, and be sorely buffeted, but God will not leave him in his hands, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.13">1 Cor. x. 13</reference>. (2.) He shall not prevail as a law-adversary: <hi type="italic">God will not condemn him when he is judged,</hi> though urged to do it by the accuser of the brethren, who <hi type="italic">accuses them before our God day and night.</hi> His false accusations will be thrown out, as those exhibited against Joshua (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.1-Zech.3.2">Zech. iii. 1, 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">The Lord rebuke thee, O Satan! It is God that justifies,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect?</hi>
entries.c2f9f3d51a46fec6be367b62e9e7023fa51efe5b: <div eID="gen11050" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Exhortations and Promises.</title> <div sID="gen11051" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">34</hi> Wait on the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and keep his way, and he shall exalt thee to inherit the land: when the wicked are cut off, thou shalt see <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">35</hi> I have seen the wicked in great power, and spreading himself like a green bay tree. <hi type="super">36</hi> Yet he passed away, and, lo, he <hi type="italic">was</hi> not: yea, I sought him, but he could not be found. <hi type="super">37</hi> Mark the perfect <hi type="italic">man,</hi> and behold the upright: for the end of <hi type="italic">that</hi> man <hi type="italic">is</hi> peace. <hi type="super">38</hi> But the transgressors shall be destroyed together: the end of the wicked shall be cut off. <hi type="super">39</hi> But the salvation of the righteous <hi type="italic">is</hi> of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="italic">he is</hi> their strength in the time of trouble. <hi type="super">40</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall help them, and deliver them: he shall deliver them from the wicked, and save them, because they trust in him. <div eID="gen11051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11052" type="x-p"/> The psalmist's conclusion of this sermon (for that is the nature of this poem) is of the same purport with the whole, and inculcates the same things. <div eID="gen11052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11053" type="x-p"/> I. The duty here pressed upon us is still the same (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wait on the Lord and keep his way.</hi> Duty is ours, and we must mind it and make conscience of it, keep God's way and never turn out of it nor loiter in it, keep close, keep going; but events are God's and we must refer ourselves to him for the disposal of them; we must wait on the Lord, attend the motions of his providence, carefully observe them, and conscientiously accommodate ourselves to them. If we make conscience of <hi type="italic">keeping God's way,</hi> we may with cheerfulness wait on him and commit to him our way; and we shall find him a good Master both to his working servants and to his waiting servants. <div eID="gen11053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11054" type="x-p"/> II. The reasons to enforce this duty are much the same too, taken from the certain destruction of the wicked and the certain salvation of the righteous. This good man, being tempted to envy the prosperity of the wicked, that he might fortify himself against the temptation, <hi type="italic">goes into the sanctuary of God</hi> and leads us thither (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">Ps. lxxiii. 17</reference>); there he understands their end, and thence gives us to understand it, and, by comparing that with the end of the righteous, baffles the temptation and puts it to silence. Observe, <div eID="gen11054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11055" type="x-p"/> 1. The misery of the wicked at last, however they may prosper awhile: <hi type="italic">The end of the wicked shall be cut off</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.38">v. 38</reference>); and that cannot be well that will undoubtedly end so ill. The wicked, in their end, will be cut off from all good and all hopes of it; a final period will be put to all their joys, and they will be for ever separated from the fountain of life to all evil. (1.) Some instances of the remarkable ruin of wicked people David had himself observed in this world—that the pomp and prosperity of sinners would not secure them from the judgments of God when their day should come to fall (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.36">v. 36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.35">35</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have seen a wicked man</hi> (the word is singular), suppose Saul or Ahithophel (for David was an old man when he penned this psalm), <hi type="italic">in great power, formidable</hi> (so some render it), <hi type="italic">the terror of the mighty in the land of the living,</hi> carrying all before him with a high hand, and seeming to be firmly fixed and finely flourishing, <hi type="italic">spreading himself like a green bay-tree,</hi> which produces all leaves and no fruit; like a native home-born Israelite (so Dr. Hammond), likely to take root. But what became of him? Eliphaz, long before, had learned, when he saw the foolish taking root, to curse his habitation, <reference osisRef="Job.5.3">Job v. 3</reference>. And David saw cause for it; for this bay-tree withered away as soon as the fig-tree. Christ cursed: <hi type="italic">He passed away as a dream,</hi> as a shadow, such was he and all the pomp and power he was so proud of. He was gone in an instant: <hi type="italic">He was not; I sought him</hi> with wonder, <hi type="italic">but he could not be found.</hi> He had acted his part and then quitted the stage, and there was no miss of him. (2.) The total and final ruin of sinners, of all sinners, will shortly be made as much a spectacle to the saints as they are now sometimes made a spectacle to the world (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">When the wicked are cut off</hi> (and cut off they certainly will be) <hi type="italic">thou shalt see it,</hi> with awful adorations of the divine justice. <hi type="italic">The transgressors shall be destroyed together,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.38">v. 38</reference>. In this world God singles out here one sinner and there another, out of many, to be made an example <hi type="italic">in terrorem—as a warning;</hi> but in the day of judgment there will be a general destruction of all the transgressors, and not one shall escape. Those that have sinned together shall be damned together. <hi type="italic">Bind them in bundles, to burn them.</hi> <div eID="gen11055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11056" type="x-p"/> 2. The blessedness of the righteous, at last. Let us see what will be the end of God's poor despised people. (1.) Preferment. There have been times the iniquity of which has been such that men's piety has hindered their preferment in this world, and put them quite out of the way of raising estates; but those that keep God's way may be assured that in due time he will <hi type="italic">exalt them, to inherit the land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.34">v. 34</reference>); he will advance them to a place in the heavenly mansions, to dignity, and honour, and true wealth, in the New Jerusalem, to inherit that good land, that land of promise, of which Canaan was a type; he will exalt them above all contempt and danger. (2.) Peace, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.37">v. 37</reference>. Let all people <hi type="italic">mark the perfect man, and behold the upright;</hi> take notice of him to admire him and imitate him, keep your eye upon him to observe what comes of him, and you will find that <hi type="italic">the end of that man is peace.</hi> Sometimes the latter end of his days proves more comfortable to him than the beginning was; the storms blow over, and he is comforted again, after the time that he was afflicted. However, if all his days continue dark and cloudy, perhaps his dying day may prove comfortable to him and his sun may set in brightness; or, if it should set under a cloud, yet his future state will be peace, everlasting peace. Those that walk in their uprightness while they live shall enter into peace when they die, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.2">Isa. lvii. 2</reference>. A peaceful death has concluded the troublesome life of many a good man; and all is well that thus ends everlastingly well. Balaam himself wished that his death and his last end might be like that of the righteous <reference osisRef="Num.23.10">Num. xxiii. 10</reference>. (3.) Salvation, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.39-Ps.37.40">v. 39, 40</reference>. <hi type="italic">The salvation of the righteous</hi> (which may be applied to the great salvation of which <hi type="italic">the prophets enquired and searched diligently,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.10">1 Pet. i. 10</reference>) <hi type="italic">is of the Lord;</hi> it will be the Lord's doing. The eternal salvation, that salvation of God which those shall see that <hi type="italic">order their conversation aright</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.23">Ps. l. 23</reference>), is likewise of the Lord. And he that intends Christ and heaven for them will be a God all-sufficient to them: <hi type="italic">He is their strength in time of trouble,</hi> to support them under it and carry them through it. <hi type="italic">He shall help them and deliver them,</hi> help them to do their duties, to bear their burdens, and to maintain their spiritual conflicts, help them to bear their troubles well and get good by them, and, in due time, shall deliver them out of their troubles. He shall deliver them from the wicked that would overwhelm them and swallow them up, shall secure them there, where the wicked cease from troubling. He shall <hi type="italic">save them,</hi> not only keep them safe, but make them happy, <hi type="italic">because they trust in him,</hi> not because they have merited it from him, but because they have committed themselves to him and reposed a confidence in him, and have thereby honoured him.  <chapter eID="Ps.37"/> <div eID="gen11056" type="x-p"/>

entries.4df8d98767c702b3403aa723fccce42fa5f3b134: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5874"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 37</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.1-Ps.37.40">Psa 37:1-40</reference>. A composed and uniform trust in God and a constant course of integrity are urged in view of the blessedness of the truly pious, contrasted in various aspects with the final ruin of the wicked. Thus the wisdom and justice of God's providence are vindicated, and its seeming inequalities, which excite the cavils of the wicked and the distrust of the pious, are explained. David's personal history abundantly illustrates the Psalm.</title> <div sID="gen8938" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5874"/>1-2. The general sentiment of the whole Psalm is expressed. The righteous need not be vexed by the prosperity of the wicked; for it is transient, and their destiny undesirable. <div eID="gen8938" type="x-p"/>
entries.9704f84dc05d904c300a7070df654512a1b0f00e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5875"/><div sID="gen8939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5875"/><hi type="bold">3. Trust--</hi>sure of safety.<div eID="gen8939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8940" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shalt thou dwell--</hi>or, "dwell thou"; repose quietly.<div eID="gen8940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">verily ... fed--</hi>or, "feed on truth," God's promise (<reference osisRef="Ps.36.5">Psa 36:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Hos.12.1">Ho 12:1</reference>). <div eID="gen8941" type="x-p"/>

entries.3b34033d7b677b10ec24ac3e208985e37a03dd19: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5892"/><div sID="gen8964" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5892"/><hi type="bold">26. his seed is blessed--</hi>literally, "for a blessing" (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.2">Ge 12:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.21.6">Psa 21:6</reference>). entries.4d92834e5d4cea8c2c98f77b412ab90084f33818: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5902"/><div sID="gen8974" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5902"/><hi type="bold">39-40. strength--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.27.1">Psa 27:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.28.8">28:8</reference>).<div eID="gen8974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trouble--</hi>straits (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.9">Psa 9:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.1">10:1</reference>).
