entries.87f745c059687bcf4c8850e5bdc0f6f9403e52bd: <div eID="gen19752" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19753" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19754" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19754" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19753" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19755" type="x-p"/> Godly directions for those who are in adversity not to envy the prosperity of the wicked, because it is superficial, and of short duration, vv. 1-22; to put their confidence in God, and live to his glory, as this is the sure way to be happy in this life, and in that which is to come, vv. 23-40. <div eID="gen19755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19756" type="x-p"/> In the title this Psalm is attributed to David by the Hebrew, and by most of the Versions: but it is more likely it was intended as an instructive and consoling ode for the captives in Babylon, who might feel themselves severely tempted when they saw those idolaters in prosperity; and themselves, who worshipped the true God, in affliction and slavery. They are comforted with the prospect of speedy deliverance; and their return to their own land is predicted in not less than ten different places in this Psalm. <div eID="gen19756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19757" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is one of the acrostic or alphabetical kind: but it differs from those we have already seen, in having two verses under each letter; the first only exhibiting the alphabetical letter consecutively. There are a few anomalies in the Psalm. The hemistich, which should begin with the letter ע ain, has now a ל lamed prefixed to the word with which it begins, לעולם leolam; and the hemistich which should begin with ת tau (<reference osisRef="Psa.37.39">Psa 37:39</reference>) has now a ו vau prefixed, ותשועת utheshuath. It appears also that the letters ד daleth, כ caph, and ק koph, have each lost a hemistich; and ע ain, half a one. The manner ill which this Psalm is printed in Dr. Kennicott's Hebrew Bible gives a full view of all these particulars. To the English reader some slighter differences may appear; but it should be observed, that the verses in our English Bibles are not always divided as those in the Hebrew. In all the Psalms that have a title, the title forms the first verse in the Hebrew; but our translation does not acknowledge any of those titles as a part of the Psalm, and very properly leaves them out of the enumeration of the verses. <div eID="gen19757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19758" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19759" type="x-p"/> Fret not thyself because of evil doers - It is as foolish as it is wicked to repine or be envious at the prosperity of others. Whether they are godly or ungodly, it is God who is the dispenser of the bounty they enjoy; and, most assuredly, he has a right to do what he will with his own. To be envious in such a case, is to arraign the providence of God. And it is no small condescension in the Almighty to reason with such persons as he does in this Psalm.
entries.3a3355614629306dfaf83b6945819e694f181512: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen19759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19760" type="x-p"/> For they shall soon be cut down - They have their portion in this life; and their enjoyment of it cannot be long, for their breath is but a vapor that speedily vanishes away. They fall before death, as the greensward does before the scythe of the mower.
entries.89b184a2f47d4852dc0402dbe15e3c25cbd3c4fa: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen19760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19761" type="x-p"/> Dwell in the land - Do not flee to foreign climes to escape from that providence which, for thy own good, denies thee affluence in thy own country. <div eID="gen19761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19762" type="x-p"/> And verily thou shalt be fed - God will provide for thee the necessaries of life: its conveniences might damp thy intellect in its inventions, and lead thee into idleness; and its superfluities would induce thee to pamper thy passions till the concerns of thy soul would be absorbed in those of the flesh and, after having lived an animal life, thou mightest die without God, and perish everlastingly. <div eID="gen19762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19763" type="x-p"/> The original, ורעה אמונה ureeh emunah, might be translated, "and feed by faith." The Septuagint has και ποιμανθησῃ επι τῳ πλουτῳ αυτης, and thou shalt feed upon its riches. The Vulgate Ethiopic, and Arabic, are the same. The Syriac, seek faith. The Chaldee, be strong in the faith. The Anglo-Saxon, and feeded thou shalt be in its welfare. Old Psalter, and thu sal be fed in ryches of it. But it is probable that אמונה emunah here signifies security. And thou shalt be fed in security. <div eID="gen19763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19764" type="x-p"/> Dr. Delaney supposed that the Psalm might have been written by David in the behalf of Mephibosheth, who, being falsely aecused by his servant Ziba, had formed the resolution to leave a land where he had met with such bad treatment. David, being convinced of his innocence, entreats him to dwell in the land, with the assurance of plenty and protection. It is more likely that it is addressed to the captives in Babylon; and contains the promise that they shall return to their own land, and again enjoy peace and plenty.
entries.53acf8b3e20783feb28ac769ca9a6b56fbbf1f99: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen19764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19765" type="x-p"/> Delight thyself also in the Lord - Expect all thy happiness from him, and seek it in him. <div eID="gen19765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19766" type="x-p"/> The desires of thine heart - משאלות mishaloth, the petitions. The godly man never indulges a desire which he cannot form into a prayer to God.
entries.11ca57e7d534f485d975337ae0ac2aa961e8c174: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19767" type="x-p"/> Commit thy way unto the Lord - גול על יהוה gol al Yehovah, Roll thy way upon the Lord: probably, a metaphor taken from the camel, who lies down till his load be rolled upon him. <div eID="gen19767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19768" type="x-p"/> He shall bring it to pass - יעשה yaaseh, "He will work." Trust God, and he will work for thee.
entries.8d6237da3f548b01e62ea123b92ad4afec3f6dfc: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen19768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19769" type="x-p"/> Thy righteousness as the light - As God said in the beginning, "Let there be light, and there was light;" so he shall say, Let thy innocence appear, and it will appear as suddenly and as evident as the light was at the beginning.
entries.ba93f09a1462c32de864981344620b9607fa4e25: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen19769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19770" type="x-p"/> Rest in the Lord - דום dom, "be silent, be dumb." Do not find fault with thy Maker; he does all things well for others, he will do all things well for thee. <div eID="gen19770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19771" type="x-p"/> And wait patiently for him - והתחולל לו vehithcholel lo, and set thyself to expect him; and be determined to expect, or wait for him. Such is the import of a verb in the hithpoel conjugation. <div eID="gen19771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19772" type="x-p"/> A heathen gives good advice on a similar subject: - <div eID="gen19772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19773" type="x-p"/> Nil ergo optabunt homines? Si consilium vis, <div eID="gen19773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19774" type="x-p"/> Permittes ipsis expendere Numinibus, quid <div eID="gen19774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19775" type="x-p"/> Conveniat nobis, rebusque sit utile nostris. <div eID="gen19775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19776" type="x-p"/> Nam pro jucundis aptissima quaeque dabunt Di. <div eID="gen19776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19777" type="x-p"/> Carior est illis homo, quam sibi. <div eID="gen19777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19778" type="x-p"/> Juv. Sat. 10:346. "What then remains? Are we deprived of will? <div eID="gen19778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19779" type="x-p"/> Must we not wish, for fear of wishing ill? <div eID="gen19779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19780" type="x-p"/> Receive my counsel, and securely move; <div eID="gen19780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19781" type="x-p"/> Intrust thy pastime to the powers above. <div eID="gen19781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19782" type="x-p"/> Leave them to manage for thee, and to grant <div eID="gen19782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19783" type="x-p"/> What their unerring wisdom sees thee want. <div eID="gen19783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19784" type="x-p"/> In goodness, as in greatness, they excel: <div eID="gen19784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19785" type="x-p"/> Ah, that we loved ourselves but half so well!" <div eID="gen19785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19786" type="x-p"/> Dryden.
entries.a8b805cf9eb4f255ae799e1c23791199496227fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen19786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19787" type="x-p"/> They shall inherit the earth - The word ארץ arets, throughout this Psalm, should be translated land, not earth; for it is most probable that it refers to the land of Judea; and in this verse there is a promise of their return thither.
entries.05062431f73a2c5a1a6c1f3c95e4831454bb39c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen19787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19788" type="x-p"/> For yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be - A prediction of the destruction of Babylon. This empire was now in its splendor; and the captives lived to see it totally overturned by Cyrus, so that even the shadow of its power did not remain. <div eID="gen19788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19789" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt diligently consider his place - ואיננו veeynennu, and he is not. The ruler is killed; the city is taken; and the whole empire is overthrown, in one night! And now even the place where Babylon stood cannot be ascertained.
entries.d5ddee1f5527a6cf28afae7fed8fa25b7923a598: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen19789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19790" type="x-p"/> But the meek - ענוים anavim, the afflicted, the poor Jewish captives. <div eID="gen19790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19791" type="x-p"/> Shall inherit the earth - ארץ arets, the land of Judea given by God himself as an inheritance to their fathers, and to their posterity for ever. See <reference osisRef="Psa.37.9">Psa 37:9</reference>.
entries.d4a3e49db283bf767bdc8abcece32b32654b964e: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen19791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19792" type="x-p"/> He seeth that his day is coming - The utter desolation of your oppressors is at hand. All this may be said of every wicked man.
entries.8230a5e211c42964b06bcf7d80ec008443051669: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen19792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19793" type="x-p"/> The wicked have drawn out the sword - There is an irreconcilable enmity in the souls of sinners against the godly; and there is much evidence that the idolatrous Babylonians whetted their tongue like a sword, and shot out their arrows, even bitter words, to malign the poor captives, and to insult them in every possible way.
entries.e24524262793d4eae6fd301aaaf8b9ffb99fbb70: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen19793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19794" type="x-p"/> Their sword shall enter into their own heart - All their execrations and maledictions shall fall upon themselves, and their power to do mischief shall be broken.
entries.0f57ff42bc1f1a7f872f14e5bd8d5d579c73655f: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen19794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19795" type="x-p"/> A little that a righteous man hath - This is a solid maxim. <div eID="gen19795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19796" type="x-p"/> Whatever a good man has, has God's blessing in it; even the blessings of the wicked are cursed.
entries.93d50250bc30b212c07670584a5cdeda94c09fbf: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen19796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19797" type="x-p"/> The arms of the wicked - Their power to do evil. Of this they are often deprived. Talents lent and abused shall be resumed, and the misuser called to a severe account by the Lord of the talents.
entries.717103255e89adeb3acf05905cfe53c77efd1951: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen19797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19798" type="x-p"/> The Lord knoweth the days of the upright - He is acquainted with all his circumstances, severings, and ability to bear them; and he will either shorten his trials or increase his power. The Lord also approves of the man and his concerns; and his inheritance shall be for ever. He shall have God for his portion, here and hereafter. This is probably another indirect promise to the captives that they shall be restored to their own land. See <reference osisRef="Psa.37.11">Psa 37:11</reference>.
entries.952d8f812c53e4d1ff91a712ef3789340432bc56: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen19798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19799" type="x-p"/> They shall not be ashamed - They have expressed strong confidence in the Lord; and he shall so work in their behalf that their enemies shall never be able to say, "Ye have trusted in your God, and yet your enemies have prevailed over you." No; for even in the days of famine they shall be satisfied.
entries.1d7c38901fd05e6fb0e55c0ba6749d21413f7812: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen19799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19800" type="x-p"/> The enemies of the Lord shall be as the fat of lambs - This verse has given the critics some trouble. Several of the Versions read thus: "But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they are exalted to honor, shall vanish; like smoke they vanish." If we follow the Hebreto, it intimates that they shall consume as the fat of lambs. That is, as the fat is wholly consumed in sacrifices by the fire on the altar, so shall they consume away in the fire of God's wrath.
entries.bf975613234d44a1c05ee199510728ac118b33b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen19800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19801" type="x-p"/> The wicked borroweth - Is often reduced to penury, and is obliged to become debtor to those whom he before despised. <div eID="gen19801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19802" type="x-p"/> And payeth not again - May refuse to do it, because he is a wicked man; or be unable to do it, because he is reduced to beggary. <div eID="gen19802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19803" type="x-p"/> But the righteous showeth mercy - Because he has received mercy from God, therefore he shows mercy to men. And even to his enemies he showeth mercy, and giveth; his heart being disposed to it by the influence of Divine grace and his hand being enabled to do it by the blessing of God's providence.
entries.89de7e38111f689b67effebee7c7c51e8f43421e: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen19803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19804" type="x-p"/> Shall inherit the earth - ארץ arets the land, as before. See <reference osisRef="Psa.37.11">Psa 37:11</reference>. <div eID="gen19804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19805" type="x-p"/> Shall be cut off - A wicked Jew shall meet with the same fate as a wicked Babylonian; and a wicked Christian shall fare no better.
entries.7735f3d607aa6b0b75b7ef209f040a83360bbc85: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen19805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19806" type="x-p"/> The steps of a good man are ordered by the Lord - There is nothing for good in the text. גבר geber is the original word, and it properly signifies a strong man, a conqueror or hero; and it appears to be used here to show, that even the most powerful must be supported by the Lord, otherwise their strength and courage will be of little avail. <div eID="gen19806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19807" type="x-p"/> And he delighteth in his way - When his steps are ordered by the Lord, he delighteth in his way, because it is that into which his own good Spirit has directed him. Or, the man delights in God's way - in the law and testimonies of his Maker.
entries.d3d1ed69f8c7e3f1b92a2dbd2d3b12bb6e43402a: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen19807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19808" type="x-p"/> Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down - The original is short and emphatic כי יפל לא יוטל ki yippol, lo yutal, which the Chaldee translates, "Though he should fall into sickness, he shall not die;" for which the reason is given, because the Lord sustains by his hand. Though he may for a time fall under the power of his adversaries, as the Jews have done under the Babylonish captivity, he shall not be forsaken. The right hand of God shall sustain him in his afflictions and distresses; and at last God will give him a happy issue out of them all. Neither the tent nor any of the Versions intimate that a falling into sin is meant; but a falling into trouble, difficulty, etc.
entries.88e959b940dfdc2c69af33b5826b4335b9335bcb: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen19808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19809" type="x-p"/> I have been young, and now am old - I believe this to be literally true in all cases. I am now grey-headed myself; I have traveled in different countries, and have had many opportunities of seeing and conversing with religious people in all situations in life; and I have not, to my knowledge, seen one instance to the contrary. I have seen no righteous man forsaken, nor any children of the righteous begging their bread. God puts this honor upon all that fear him; and thus careful is he of them, and of their posterity.
entries.47c708fac7e98d2ee04d5c7092fbef613a997ec5: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen19809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19810" type="x-p"/> He is ever merciful and lendeth - כל היום חונן kol haiyom chonen, "all the day he is compassionate." He is confirmed in the habit of godliness: he feels for the distresses of men, and is ready to divide and distribute to all that are in necessity. <div eID="gen19810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19811" type="x-p"/> And his seed is blessed - The preceding words were not spoken casually; his seed, his posterity, is blessed; therefore they are not abandoned to beg their bread.
entries.dc373d79392e0d10e7d9f69595f4eb6aecae701a: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen19811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19812" type="x-p"/> Depart from evil, and do good - Seeing the above is so, depart from all evil - avoid all sin; and let not this be sufficient, do good. The grace of God ever gives this two-fold power to all who receive it; strength to overcome evil, and strength to do that which is right. <div eID="gen19812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19813" type="x-p"/> Dwell for evermore - Be for ever an inhabitant of God's house. This may be also a promise of return to their own land, and of permanent residence there. See <reference osisRef="Psa.37.9">Psa 37:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.37.11">Psa 37:11</reference>, etc.
entries.f159b5f6f30a0062db75061e81014db78daa6f65: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen19813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19814" type="x-p"/> Forsaketh not his saints - את חטידיו eth chasidaiv, his merciful or compassionate ones; those who, through love to him and all mankind, are ever ready to give of their substance to the poor. <div eID="gen19814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19815" type="x-p"/> But the seed of the wicked shall be cut off - The children who follow the wicked steps of wicked parents shall, like their parents, be cut off. God's judgments descend to posterity, as well as his mercies.
entries.7949c9ec68d8a37a7e5038faa251b018bb8a8460: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen19815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19816" type="x-p"/> The righteous shall inherit the land - If this be not another promise of return to their own land, from that of their captivity, it must be spiritually understood, and refer to their eternal dwelling with God in glory.
entries.fce66523e5739f8d5baf66aadbcad5da3da7b8f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen19816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19817" type="x-p"/> The mouth of the righteous speaketh wisdom - Foolish and corrupt conversation cannot come out of their mouth. They are taught of God, and they speak according to the wisdom that is from above.
entries.d2306df04ff6aab462166ea2b74277f78ead4b54: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen19817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19818" type="x-p"/> The law of his God is in his heart - The Lord promised that a time should come in which he would make a new covenant with the house of Israel; he would put his laws in their minds, and in their hearts he would write them. This is fulfilled in the case above. <div eID="gen19818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19819" type="x-p"/> None of his steps shall slide - His holy heart always dictates to his eyes, his mouth, his hands, and his feet. The precepts which direct his conduct are not only written in his Bible, but also in his heart.
entries.3e0c79d4f1db966f2f5c3d9335338971703b6e0b: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen19819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19820" type="x-p"/> The wicked watcheth the righteous, and seeketh to slay him - Similar to what is said <reference osisRef="Psa.37.8">Psa 37:8</reference> : "The wicked plotteth against the righteous." But it is added, <reference osisRef="Psa.37.33">Psa 37:33</reference> : "The Lord will not leave him in his hands;" he will confound his devices, and save his own servants.
entries.982e079c0ee09905a6668993b2d6b3a15775b88a: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen19820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19821" type="x-p"/> Wait on the Lord, and keep his way - This is the true mode of waiting on God which the Scripture recommends; keeping God's way - using all his ordinances, and living in the spirit of obedience. He who waits thus is sure to have the farther blessings of which he is in pursuit. קוה kavah, to wait, implies the extension of a right line from one point to another. The first point is the human heart; the line is its intense desire; and the last point is God, to whom this heart extends this straight line of earnest desire to be filled with the fullness of the blessing of the Gospel of peace. <div eID="gen19821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19822" type="x-p"/> And he shall exalt thee to inherit the land - If ye keep his way, and be faithful to him in your exile, he will exalt you, lift you up from your present abject state, to inherit the land of your fathers. See before, <reference osisRef="Psa.37.9">Psa 37:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.37.11">Psa 37:11</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen19822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19823" type="x-p"/> When the wicked are cut off, thou shalt see it - They did see the destruction of the Babylonish king, Belshazzar, and his empire; and it was in consequence of that destruction that they were enlarged.
entries.e55b1f188e75cd62a1cc4134e27ed756006a39c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen19823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19824" type="x-p"/> I have seen the wicked in great power, and spreading himself like a green bay-tree - Does not this refer to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and to the vision he had of the great tree which was in the midst of the earth, the head of which reached up to heaven? See <reference osisRef="Dan.4.10">Dan 4:10</reference>, etc.
entries.082c0b7963484db3a07ecc4986a4a6a7ada3d694: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen19824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19825" type="x-p"/> Yet he passed away - Both Nebuchadnezzar and his wicked successor, Belshazzar; and on the destruction of the latter, when God had weighed him in the balance, and found him wanting, numbered his days, and consigned him to death, his kingdom was delivered to the Medes and Persians; and thus the Babylonian empire was destroyed.
entries.639ffa30352a08cb51384a1e8e2b0af89957f4ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen19825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19826" type="x-p"/> Mark the perfect man - Him who is described above. Take notice of him: he is perfect in his soul, God having saved him from all sin, and filled him with his own love and image. And he is upright in his conduct; and his end, die when he may or where he may, is peace, quietness, and assurance for ever. <div eID="gen19826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19827" type="x-p"/> Almost all the Versions translate the Hebrew after this manner: Preserve innocence, and keep equity in view; for the man of peace shall leave a numerous posterity. <div eID="gen19827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19828" type="x-p"/> Bishop Horsley thus translates: "Keep (thy) loyalty, and look well to (thy) integrity; for a posterity is (appointed) for the perfect man." He comes nearer to the original in his note on this verse: "Keep innocency, and regard uprightness; for the perfect man hath a posterity:" "but the rebellious shall be destroyed together; the posterity of the wicked shall be cut off," <reference osisRef="Psa.37.38">Psa 37:38</reference>. <div eID="gen19828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19829" type="x-p"/> Dr. Kennicott's note is," אחרית acharith, which we render latter end, is posterity, <reference osisRef="Psa.109.13">Psa 109:13</reference>. The wicked and all his race to be destroyed, the pious man to have a numerous progeny, see his sons' sons to the third and fourth generation. See <reference osisRef="Job.8.19">Job 8:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.18.13-Job.18.20">Job 18:13-20</reference>." <div eID="gen19829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19830" type="x-p"/> I think the original cannot possibly bear our translation. I shall produce it here, with the literal version of Montanus: - pax viro novissimum quia; rectum vide et, integrum cutodi שלום לאיש אחרית כי ישר וראה תם שמר The nearest translation to this is that of the Septuagint and Vulgate: Φυλασσε ακακιαν, και ιδε ευθυτητα, ὁτι εστιν εγκαταλειμμα ανθρωπῳ ειρηνικῳ· Custodi innocentiam, et vide aequitatem; quoniam, sunt reliquiae homini pacifico. "Preserve innocence, and behold equity; seeing there is a posterity to the pacific man." The Syriac says, "Observe simplicity, and choose rectitude; seeing there is a good end to the man of peace." The reader may choose. Our common version, in my opinion, cannot be sustained. The <reference osisRef="Psa.37.38">Psa 37:38</reference> seems to confirm the translation of the Septuagint and the Vulgate, which are precisely the same in meaning; therefore I have given one translation for both. <div eID="gen19830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19831" type="x-p"/> The old Psalter deserves a place also: Kepe unnoyandnes, and se evenhede; for tha celykes er til a pesful man.
entries.6b714c138902df09b28992c69eac6cd74bd84976: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen19831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19832" type="x-p"/> The salvation of the righteous is of the Lord - It is the Lord who made them righteous, by blotting out their sins, and infusing his Holy Spirit into their hearts; and it is by his grace they are continually sustained, and finally brought to the kingdom of glory: "He is their strength in the time of trouble."
entries.3cbf505899cdd9a5e6b16185db9bae6481058713: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen19832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19833" type="x-p"/> The Lord - shall deliver them - For they are always exposed to trials, and liable to fall. <div eID="gen19833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19834" type="x-p"/> Because they trust in him - They keep faith, prayer, love, and obedience in continual exercise. They continue to believe in, love, and obey God; and he continues to save them.  <chapter eID="Ps.37"/> <div eID="gen19834" type="x-p"/>

entries.0b86ee63d3475c4f87b58ce46768bd149dc4e50e: <div eID="gen9406" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Seeming Prosperity of the Wicked, and the Real Prosperity of the Godly</title> <div sID="gen9407" type="x-p"/> The bond of connection between <reference osisRef="Ps.36.1-Ps.36.12">Psa 36:1-12</reference> and 37 is their similarity of contents, which here and there extends even to accords of expression. The fundamental thought running through the whole Psalm is at once expressed in the opening verses: Do not let the prosperity of the ungodly be a source of vexation to thee, but wait on the Lord; for the prosperity of the ungodly will suddenly come to an end, and the issue determines between the righteous and the unrighteous. Hence Tertullian calls this Psalm <hi type="italic">providentiae speculum</hi>; Isodore, <hi type="italic">potio contra murmur</hi>; and Luther, <hi type="italic">vestis piorum, cui adscriptum: Hic Sanctorum patientia est</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.12">Rev 14:12</reference>). This fundamental thought the poet does not expand in strophes of ordinary compass, but in shorter utterances of the proverbial form following the order of the letters of the alphabet, and not without some repetitions and recurrences to a previous thought, in order to impress it still more convincingly and deeply upon the mind. The Psalm belongs therefore to the series Ps 9 and <reference osisRef="Ps.10.1">Psa 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">Psa 25:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.1">Psa 34:1</reference>, - all alphabetical Psalms of David, of whose language, cheering, high-flown, thoughtful, and at the same time so easy and unartificial, and withal elegant, this Psalm is fully worthy. The structure of the proverbial utterances is almost entirely tetrastichic; though ד, כ, and ק are tristichs, and ח (which is twice represented, though perhaps unintentionally), נ, and ת are pentastichs. The ע is apparently wanting; but, on closer inspection, the originally separated strophes ס and ע are only run into one another by the division of the verses. The ע strophe begins with לעולם, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.28">Psa 37:28</reference></hi>, and forms a tetrastich, just like the ס. The fact that the preposition ל stands before the letter next in order need not confuse one. The ת, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.39">Psa 37:39</reference>, also begins with ותשׁועת. The homogeneous beginnings, זמם רשׁע, לוה רשׁע, צופה רשׁע, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.12">Psa 37:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.21">Psa 37:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.32">Psa 37:32</reference>, seem, as Hitzig remarks, to be designed to give prominence to the pauses in the succession of the proverbial utterances.
entries.c7c1c606c9cf365b2511641dd38da97742ef1128: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.1-Ps.37.2">Psa 37:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen9407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9408" type="x-p"/> Olshausen observes, “The poet keeps entirely to the standpoint of the old Hebrew doctrine of recompense, which the Book of Job so powerfully refutes.” But, viewed in the light of the final issue, all God’s government is really in a word righteous recompense; and the Old Testament theodicy is only inadequate in so far as the future, which adjusts all present inconsistencies, is still veiled. Meanwhile the punitive justice of God does make itself manifest, as a rule, in the case of the ungodly even in the present world; even their dying is usually a fearful end to their life’s prosperity. This it is which the poet means here, and which is also expressed by Job himself in the Book of Job, Job 27:1. With התחרה, to grow hot or angry (distinct from תּחרה, to emulate, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5">Jer 12:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.15">Jer 22:15</reference>), alternates קנּא, to get into a glow, <hi type="italic">excandescentia</hi>, whether it be the restrained heat of sullen envy, or the incontrollable heat of impetuous zeal which would gladly call down fire from heaven. This first distich has been transferred to the Book of Proverbs, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.19">Pro 24:19</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.23.17">Pro 23:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.1">Pro 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.31">Pro 3:31</reference>; and in general we may remark that this Psalm is one of the Davidic patterns for the Salomonic gnome system. The form ימּלוּ is, according to Gesenius, Olshausen, and Hitzig, <hi type="italic">fut. Kal</hi> of מלל, cognate אמל, they wither away, pausal form for ימּלוּ like יתּממוּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.28">Psa 102:28</reference>; but the signification to cut off also is secured to the verb מלל by the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נמל, <reference osisRef="Gen.17.11">Gen 17:11</reference>, whence <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. ימּלוּ = ימּלּוּ; vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.14.2">Job 14:2</reference>; Job 18:16. ירק דּשׁא is a genitival combination: the green (<hi type="italic">viror</hi>) of young vigorous vegetation.
entries.12e1ac178944335316948cb4ed34557b8507cade: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.3-Ps.37.4">Psa 37:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen9408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9409" type="x-p"/> The “land” is throughout this Psalm the promised possession (<hi type="italic">Heilsgut</hi>), viz., the land of Jahve’s presence, which has not merely a glorious past, but also a future rich in promises; and will finally, ore perfectly than under Joshua, become the inheritance of the true Israel. It is therefore to be explained: enjoy the quiet sure habitation which God gives thee, and diligently cultivate the virtue of faithfulness. The two imperatives in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.3">Psa 37:3</reference></hi>, since there are two of them (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.37.27">Psa 37:27</reference>) and the first is without any conjunctive <hi type="italic">Waw</hi>, have the appearance of being continued admonitions, not promises; and consequently אמוּנה is not an adverbial accusative as in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.75">Psa 119:75</reference> (Ewald), but the object to רעה, to pasture, to pursue, to practise (Syriac רדף, Hos 12:2); cf. רעה, רע, one who interests himself in any one, or anything; Beduin <hi type="italic">râ‛â = ṣâḥb</hi>, of every kind of closer relationship (<hi type="italic">Deutsch. Morgenländ. Zeitschr.</hi> v. 9). In <reference osisRef="Ps.37.4">Psa 37:4</reference>, ויתן is an apodosis: delight in Jahve (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.22.26">Job 22:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.10">Psa 27:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.14">Isa 58:14</reference>), so will He grant thee the desire (משׁאלת, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.20.5">Psa 20:5</reference>) of thy heart; for he who, entirely severed from the creature, finds his highest delight in God, cannot desire anything that is at enmity with God, but he also can desire nothing that God, with whose will his own is thoroughly blended in love, would refuse him.
entries.7ab53b99b796e9da63e70d1c7684492353d3d130: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.5-Ps.37.6">Psa 37:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen9409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9410" type="x-p"/> The lxx erroneously renders גּול (= גּל, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.9">Psa 22:9</reference>) by ἀποκάλυψον instead of ἐπίῤῥιψον, 1Pe 5:7 : roll the burden of cares of thy life’s way upon Jahve, leave the guidance of thy life entirely to Him, and to Him alone, without doing anything in it thyself: He will gloriously accomplish (all that concerns thee): עשׂה, as in Ps 22:32; 52:11; cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.16.3">Pro 16:3</reference>, and Paul Gerhardt’s <hi type="italic">Befiehl du deine Wege</hi>, “Commit thou all thy ways,” etc. The perfect in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.6">Psa 37:6</reference> is a continuation of the promissory יעשׂה. הוציא, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.10">Jer 51:10</reference>, signifies to set forth: He will bring to light thy misjudged righteousness like the light (the sun, <reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job 31:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.37.21">Job 37:21</reference>, and more especially the morning sun, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pro 4:18</reference>), which breaks through the darkness; and thy down-trodden right (משׁפּטך is the pausal form of the singular beside <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>) like the bright light of the noon-day: cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.58.10">Isa 58:10</reference>, as on <reference osisRef="Ps.37.4">Psa 37:4</reference>, Isa 58:14.
entries.b82cebfeb88b6e177d71d709afada138cfd8ca99: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.7">Psa 37:7</reference> <div eID="gen9410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9411" type="x-p"/> The verb דּמם, with its derivatives (<reference osisRef="Ps.62.2">Psa 62:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.62.6">Psa 62:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.28">Lam 3:28</reference>), denotes resignation, i.e., a quiet of mind which rests on God, renounces all self-help, and submits to the will of God. התחולל (from הוּל, to be in a state of tension, to wait) of the inward gathering of one’s self together in hope intently directed towards God, as in <hi type="italic">B. Berachoth 30b</hi> is a synonym of התחונן, and as it were reflexive of חלּה of the collecting one’s self to importunate prayer. With <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.7">Psa 37:7</reference></hi> the primary tone of the whole Psalm is struck anew. On <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.7">Psa 37:7</reference></hi> compare the definition of the mischief-maker in Pro 24:8.
entries.43958871cd5d2eadba0f8cc561d734474660796a: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.8-Ps.37.9">Psa 37:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen9411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9412" type="x-p"/> On הרף (let alone), <hi type="italic">imper. apoc. Hiph</hi>., instead of הרפּה, vid., Ges. §75, rem. 15. אך להרע is a clause to itself (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.11.24">Pro 11:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.21.5">Psa 21:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">Psa 22:16</reference>): it tends only to evil-doing, it ends only in thy involving thyself in sin. The final issue, without any need that thou shouldst turn sullen, is that the מרעים, like to whom thou dost make thyself by such passionate murmuring and displeasure, will be cut off, and they who, turning from the troublous present, make Jahve the ground and aim of their hope, shall inherit the land (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.25.13">Psa 25:13</reference>). It is the end, the final and consequently eternal end, that decides the matter.
entries.ba2947d70168382001816dda5e02a121959d91f8: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.10-Ps.37.11">Psa 37:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen9412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9413" type="x-p"/> The protasis in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.10">Psa 37:10</reference></hi> is literally: <hi type="italic">adhuc parum </hi>(<hi type="italic">temporis superest</hi>), עוד מעט ו, as e.g., <reference osisRef="Exod.23.30">Exo 23:30</reference>, and as in a similar connection מעט ו, Job 24:24. והתבּוננתּ also is a protasis with a hypothetical perfect, Ges. §155, 4, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. This promise also runs in the mouth of the Preacher on the Mount (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.5">Mat 5:5</reference>) just as the lxx renders <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.11">Psa 37:11</reference></hi>: οἱ δὲ πρᾳεῖς κληρονομήσουσι γῆν. Meekness, which is content with God, and renounces all earthly stays, will at length become the inheritor of the land, yea of the earth. Whatever God-opposed self-love may amass to itself and may seek to acquire, falls into the hands of the meek as their blessed possession.
entries.c12d908efbf4493d632fd76a094b42e9c07b7731: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.12-Ps.37.13">Psa 37:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen9413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9414" type="x-p"/> The verb זמם is construed with ל of that which is the object at which the evil devices aim. To gnash the teeth (elsewhere also: with the teeth) is, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.16">Psa 35:16</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Job.16.9">Job 16:9</reference>, a gesture of anger, not of mockery, although anger and mockery are usually found together. But the Lord, who regards an assault upon the righteous as an assault upon Himself, laughs (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.4">Psa 2:4</reference>) at the enraged schemer; for He, who orders the destinies of men, sees beforehand, with His omniscient insight into the future, his day, i.e., the day of his death (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.10">1Sa 26:10</reference>), of his visitation (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>, Oba 1:12, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.27">Jer 50:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.31">Jer 50:31</reference>).
entries.bec4a44b72c1cd54d8b6a5a56a5d680029d9eb84: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.14-Ps.37.15">Psa 37:14-15</reference> <div eID="gen9414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9415" type="x-p"/> That which corresponds to the “treading” or stringing of the bow is the drawing from the sheath or unsheathing of the sword: פּתח, <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.28">Eze 21:28</reference>, cf. Psa 55:22. The combination ישׁרי־דּרך is just like תמימי־דוך, Psa 119:1. The emphasis in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.14">Psa 37:14</reference> is upon the suffix of בלבּם: they shall perish by their own weapon. קשּׁתותם has (in Baer) a <hi type="italic">Shebâ dirimens</hi>, as also in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.28">Isa 5:28</reference> in correct texts.
entries.f59db67f8c29ecabda483867a556388d158b7b98: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.16-Ps.37.17">Psa 37:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen9415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9416" type="x-p"/> With <reference osisRef="Ps.37.16">Psa 37:16</reference> accord <reference osisRef="Prov.15.16">Pro 15:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.8">Pro 16:8</reference>, cf. Tobit 12:8. The ל of לצּדּיק is a periphrastic indication of the genitive (Ges. §115). המון is a noisy multitude, here used of earthly possessions. רבּים is not <hi type="italic">per attract</hi>. (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.38.11">Psa 38:11</reference>, הם for הוּא) equivalent to רב, but the one righteous man is contrasted with many unrighteous. The arms are here named instead of the bow in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.15">Psa 37:15</reference></hi>. He whose arms are broken can neither injure others nor help himself. Whereas Jahve does for the righteous what earthly wealth and human power cannot do: He Himself upholds them.
entries.869f6105e7a0d7e08f70952046d5b39b3e6da998: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.18-Ps.37.19">Psa 37:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen9416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9417" type="x-p"/> The life of those who love Jahve with the whole heart is, with all its vicissitudes, an object of His loving regard and of His observant providential care, <reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Psa 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.8">Psa 31:8</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1">Psa 16:1</reference>-11. He neither suffers His own to lose their heritage nor to be themselves lost to it. The αἰώνιος κληρονομία is not as yet thought of as extending into the future world, as in the New Testament. In <reference osisRef="Ps.37.19">Psa 37:19</reference> the surviving refers only to this present life.
entries.648c5ada262ce01c2c378cc91a8655fc7e3072ac: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.20">Psa 37:20</reference> <div eID="gen9417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9418" type="x-p"/> With כּי the preceding assertion is confirmed by its opposite (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">Psa 130:4</reference>). כּיקר בּרים forms a fine play in sound; יקר is a substantivized adjective like גּדל ekil evitcejda, Exo 15:16. Instead of בעשׁן, it is not to be read כּעשׁן, Hos 13:3; the ב is secured by <reference osisRef="Ps.102.4">Psa 102:4</reference>; Psa 78:33. The idea is, that they vanish into smoke, i.e., are resolved into it, or also, that they vanish in the manner of smoke, which is first thick, but then becomes thinner and thinner till it disappears (Rosenmüller, Hupfeld, Hitzig); both expressions are admissible as to fact and as to the language, and the latter is commended by בּהבל, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.33">Psa 78:33</reference>, cf. בּצלם, Psa 39:7. בעשׁן belongs to the first, regularly accented כּלוּ; for the <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> by בעשׂן is the substitute for <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>, which never can be used where at least two syllables do not precede the <hi type="italic">Silluk</hi> tone (vid., <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi> ii. 503). The second כּלוּ has the accent on the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>. for a change (Ew. §194, <hi type="italic">c</hi>), i.e., variation of the rhythm (cf. למה   למה, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.10">Psa 42:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.43.2">Psa 43:2</reference>; עורי   עורי, Jdg 5:12, and on <reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>), and in particular here on account of its pausal position (cf. ערוּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>).
entries.61da723ce53ec197baf5ec22d2d348cc18d24186: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.21-Ps.37.22">Psa 37:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen9418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9419" type="x-p"/> It is the promise expressed in <reference osisRef="Deut.15.6">Deu 15:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.12">Deu 28:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.44">Deu 28:44</reference>, which is rendered in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.21">Psa 37:21</reference> in the more universal, sententious form. לוה signifies to be bound or under obligation to any one = to borrow and to owe (<hi type="italic">nexum esse</hi>). The confirmation of <reference osisRef="Ps.37.22">Psa 37:22</reference> is not inappropriate (as Hitzig considers it, who places <reference osisRef="Ps.37.22">Psa 37:22</reference> after <reference osisRef="Ps.37.20">Psa 37:20</reference>): in that ever deeper downfall of the ungodly, and in that charitableness of the righteous, which becomes more and more easy to him by reason of his prosperity, the curse and blessing of God, which shall be revealed in the end of the earthly lot of both the righteous and the ungodly, are even now foretold. Whilst those who reject the blessing of God are cut off, the promise given to the patriarchs is fulfilled in the experience of those who are blessed of God, in all its fulness.
entries.78bd4431874fb31dc9548ead53f097f1dac60f76: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.23-Ps.37.24">Psa 37:23-24</reference> <div eID="gen9419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9420" type="x-p"/> By Jahve (מן, ἀπό, almost equivalent to ὑπό with the passive, as in <reference osisRef="Job.24.1">Job 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.11">Ecc 12:11</reference>, and in a few other passages) are a man’s steps made firm, established; not: ordered or directed (lxx, Jerome, κατευθύνεται), which, according to the extant usage of the language, would be הוּכנוּ (passive of הכין, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.9">Pro 16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.23">Jer 10:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.27.6">2Ch 27:6</reference>), whereas כּוננוּ, the <hi type="italic">Pulal</hi> of כּונן, is to be understood according to Psa 40:3. By גּבר is meant man in an emphatic sense (<reference osisRef="Job.38.3">Job 38:3</reference>), and in fact in an ethical sense; compare, on the other hand, the expression of the more general saying, “Man proposes, and God disposes,” <reference osisRef="Prov.16.9">Pro 16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.24">Pro 20:24</reference>; Jer 10:23. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.23">Psa 37:23</reference></hi> shows that it is the upright man that is meant in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.23">Psa 37:23</reference></hi>: to the way, i.e., course of life, of such an one God turns with pleasure (יחפּץ pausal change of vowel for יחפּץ): supposing he should fall, whether it be a fall arising from misfortune or from error, or both together, he is not prostrated, but Jahve upholds his hand, affords it a firm point of support or fulcrum (cf. תּמך בּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.9">Psa 63:9</reference>, and frequently), so that he can raise himself again, rise up again.
entries.002ac7b5964e4ba11ad30fe3d71e2846137c24a4: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.25-Ps.37.26">Psa 37:25-26</reference> <div eID="gen9420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9421" type="x-p"/> There is an old theological rule: <hi type="italic">promissiones corporales intelligendae sunt cum exceptione crucis et castigationis</hi>. Temporary forsakenness and destitution the Psalm does not deny: it is indeed even intended to meet the conflict of doubt which springs up in the minds of the God-fearing out of certain conditions and circumstances that are seemingly contradictory to the justice of God; and this it does, by contrasting that which in the end abides with that which is transitory, and in fact without the knowledge of any final decisive adjustment in a future world; and it only solves its problem, in so far as it is placed in the light of the New Testament, which already dawns in the Book of Ecclesiastes.
entries.ff03303d9ababca267a992b85f5cce6a4c5c9f23: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.27-Ps.37.28">Psa 37:27-28</reference> <div eID="gen9421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9422" type="x-p"/> The round of the exhortations and promises is here again reached as in Psa 37:3. The imperative שׁכן, which is there hortatory, is found here with the ו of sequence in the sense of a promise: and continue, doing such things, to dwell for ever = so shalt thou, etc. (שׁכן, pregnant as in Ps 102:29, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa 57:15</reference>). Nevertheless the imperative retains its meaning even in such instances, inasmuch as the exhortation is given to share in the reward of duty at the same time with the discharge of it. On <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.28">Psa 37:28</reference></hi> compare Psa 33:5.
entries.116212979c0ce79c4d203d0016cd048d98b0d1dc: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.30-Ps.37.31">Psa 37:30-31</reference> <div eID="gen9423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9424" type="x-p"/> The verb הגה unites in itself the two meanings of meditating and of meditative utterance (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1">Psa 2:1</reference>), just as אמר those of thinking and speaking. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.31">Psa 37:31</reference></hi> in this connection affirms the stability of the moral nature. The walk of the righteous has a fixed inward rule, for the Tôra is to him not merely an external object of knowledge and a compulsory precept; it is in his heart, and, because it is the Tôra of his God whom he loves, as the motive of his actions closely united with his own will. On תּמעד, followed by the subject in the plural, compare <reference osisRef="Ps.18.35">Psa 18:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.2">Psa 73:2</reference> <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi>.
entries.146c851ed91d0a7da3596c37713c2409b68fedd8: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.32-Ps.37.33">Psa 37:32-33</reference> <div eID="gen9424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9425" type="x-p"/> The Lord as ἀνακρίνων is, as in 1Co 4:3., put in contrast with the ἀνακρίνειν of men, or of human ἡμέρᾳ. If men sit in judgment upon the righteous, yet God, the supreme Judge, does not condemn him, but acquits him (cf. on the contrary <reference osisRef="Ps.109.7">Psa 109:7</reference>). <hi type="italic">Si condemnamur a mundo</hi>, exclaimed Tertullian to his companions in persecution, <hi type="italic">absolvimur a Deo</hi>.
entries.fad8d6a33053799604e0de3ac9442377d08ea460: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.34">Psa 37:34</reference> <div eID="gen9425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9426" type="x-p"/> Let the eye of faith directed hopefully to Jahve go on its way, without suffering thyself to be turned aside by the persecution and condemnation of the world, then He will at length raise thee out of all trouble, and cause thee to possess (לרשׁת, <hi type="italic">ut possidas et possideas</hi>) the land, as the sole lords of which the evil-doers, now cut off, conducted themselves.
entries.7ed4844b6781f9842da4a67e9d675bc40595853e: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.35-Ps.37.36">Psa 37:35-36</reference> עריץ (after the form צדּיק) is coupled with רשׁע, must as these two words alternate in <reference osisRef="Job.15.20">Job 15:20</reference> : a terror-inspiring, tyrannical evil-doer; cf. besides also Job 5:3. The participle in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.35">Psa 37:35</reference></hi> forms a clause by itself: <hi type="italic">et se diffundens</hi>, scil. <hi type="italic">erat</hi>. The lxx and Jerome translate as though it were כארז הלבנן, “like the cedars of Lebanon,” instead of כאזרח רענן. But אזרח רענן is the expression for an oak, terebinth, or the like, that has brown from time immemorial in its native soil, and has in the course of centuries attained a gigantic size in the stem, and a wide-spreading overhanging head. ויּעבר does not mean: then he vanished away (Hupfeld and others); for עבר in this sense is not suitable to a tree. Luther correctly renders it: <hi type="italic">man ging vorüber</hi>, one (they) passed by, Ges. §137, 3. The lxx, Syriac, and others, by way of lightening the difficulty, render it: then I passed by.
entries.cd56fa758cdc8d6313170d6aa58b383d0c92168c: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.37-Ps.37.38">Psa 37:37-38</reference> תּם might even be taken as neuter for תּם, and ישׂר for ישׁר; but in this case the poet would have written רעה instead of ראה; שׁמר is therefore used as, e.g., in 1Sa 1:12. By כּי that to which attention is specially called is introduced. The man of peace has a totally different lot from the evil-doer who delights in contention and persecution. As the fruit of his love of peace he has אחרית, a future, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.18">Pro 23:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.14">Pro 24:14</reference>, viz., in his posterity, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.20">Pro 24:20</reference>; whereas the apostates are altogether blotted out; not merely they themselves, but even the posterity of the ungodly is cut off, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.2">Amo 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.1">Amo 9:1</reference>; Eze 23:25. To them remains no posterity to carry forward their name, their אחרית is devoted to destruction (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.109.13">Psa 109:13</reference> with Num 24:20).
entries.4ec4bc1d9cb9488a1a92422190e4185f8078a186: <reference osisRef="Ps.37.39-Ps.37.40">Psa 37:39-40</reference> <div eID="gen9426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9427" type="x-p"/> The salvation of the righteous cometh from Jahve; it is therefore characterized, in accordance with its origin, as sure, perfect, and enduring for ever. מעוּזּם is an apposition; the <hi type="italic">plena scriptio</hi> serves, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.33">2Sa 22:33</reference>, to indicate to us that מעוז is meant in this passage to signify not a fortress, but a hiding-place, a place of protection, a refuge, in which sense Arab. <hi type="italic">ma'âd‛llh</hi> (the protection of God) and <hi type="italic">m‛âḏwjh‛llh</hi> (the protection of God’s presence) is an Arabic expression (also used as a formula of an oath); vid., moreover on Psa 31:3. The moods of sequence in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.40">Psa 37:40</reference> are <hi type="italic">aoristi gnomici</hi>. The parallelism in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.37.40">Psa 37:40</reference></hi> is progressive after the manner of the Psalms of degrees. The short confirmatory clause <hi type="italic">kichā'subo</hi> forms an expressive closing cadence.  <chapter eID="Ps.37"/> <div eID="gen9427" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 37
This psalm, the title of which shows it to have been composed by David, contains most profitable instruction. Since the faithful, so long as they pursue their earthly pilgrimage through life, see things strangely confused in the world, unless they assuaged their grief with the hope of a better issue, their courage would soon fail them. The more boldly any man despises God, and runs to every excess in wickedness, so much the more happily he seems to live. And since prosperity appears to be a token of God’s favor towards the ungodly, what conclusion, it may be said, can be drawn from this, but either that the world is governed by chance, and that fortune bears the sovereignty, or else that God makes no difference between the good and the bad? The Spirit of God accordingly confirms and strengthens us in this psalm against the assaults of such a temptation. However great the prosperity which the wicked enjoy for a time, he declares their felicity to be transient and evanescent, and that, therefore, they are miserable, while the happiness of which they boast is cursed; whereas the pious and devoted servants of God never cease to be happy, even in the midst of their greatest calamities, because God takes care of them, and at length comes to their aid in due season. This, indeed, is paradoxical, and wholly repugnant to human reason. For as good men often suffer extreme poverty, and languish long under many troubles, and are loaded with reproaches and wrongs, while the wicked and profligate triumph, and are regaled with pleasures, might we not suppose that God cares not for the things that are done on earth? It is on this account that, as I have already said, the doctrine of this psalm is so much the more profitable; because, withdrawing our thoughts from the present aspect of things, it enjoins us to confide in the providence of God, until he stretch forth his hand to help those who are his servants, and demand of the ungodly a strict account of their lives, as of thieves and robbers who have foully abused his bounty and paternal goodness.
A Psalm of David.
Psalm 37:1-6
1. Fret not thyself because of the wicked, and be not envious at the workers of iniquity: 2. For they shall soon be cut down like grass; and they shall wither as the green and tender herb. 3. Put thy trust in Jehovah, and do good; dwell in the land, and be fed in truth, [or faithfully.
“C’est, jouy des biens d’icelle en repos ferme et asseure.” — Fr. marg. “That is, enjoy the good things of it in quietness and security.”
] 4. And delight thyself in Jehovah, and he will give thee the desires of thy heart. 5. Roll [or devolve] thy ways on Jehovah, and trust in him, and he will bring it to pass. 6. And he will bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgments
“C’est, ton bon droict.” — Fr. marg. “That is, thy just cause, or thy rectitude.
as the noon day.
 
1. Fret not thyself because of the wicked. David lays down this as a general principle, that the prosperity of the wicked, in which they greatly rejoice, should on no account vex or disquiet the children of God, because it will soon fade away. On the other hand, although the people of God are afflicted for a time, yet the issue of their afflictions shall be such, that they have every reason to be contented with their lot. Now all this depends upon the providence of God; for unless we are persuaded that the world is governed by him in righteousness and truth, our minds will soon stagger, and at length entirely fail us. David then condemns two sinful affections of the mind, which are indeed closely allied, and the one of which is generated by the other. He first enjoins the faithful not to fret on account of the wicked; and, secondly, that they should not indulge an envious spirit towards them. For, in the first place, when they see the wicked enjoying prosperity, from which it might naturally be supposed that God regards not the affairs of men, there is a danger lest they should shake off the fear of God, and apostatise from the faith. Then another temptation follows, namely, that the influence of the example of the wicked excites in them a desire to involve themselves in the same wickedness with them. This is the natural sense. The Hebrew words, אל-תתחר, al-tithechar, which we have rendered, Fret not thyself, are by some translated, Do not mingle thyself with.
That is, do not enter into fellowship with.
But this interpretation is too forced, and may be disproved by the context; for in the eighth verse, where mention is expressly made of wrath and anger, it would surely be absurd to interpret in another sense the same verb which immediately follows these two words, and which is there used in the same sense and for the same end as in this first verse. In the second place, the order which David observes is very natural; for when the prosperity of the wicked has irritated our minds, we very soon begin to envy them their happiness and ease. First, then, he exhorts us to be on our guard, lest a happiness which is only transitory, or rather imaginary, should vex or disquiet us; and, secondly, lest envy should lead us to commit sin. The reason by which he enforces this exhortation is added in the following verse: for if the wicked flourish to-day like the grass of the field, to-morrow they shall be cut down and wither. We need not wonder that this similitude is often to be met with in the sacred writings, since it is so very appropriate; for we see how soon the strength of the grass decays, and that when cast down by a blast of wind, or parched with the heat of the sun, even without being cut by the hand of man, it withers away.
The fitness of this figure to express the transient and short-lived character of the prosperity of the wicked, will appear in a still more striking light when we take into consideration the great heat of the climate of Palestine.
In like manner, David tells us that the judgment of God, like a scythe in the hand of man, shall cut down the wicked, so that they shall suddenly perish.

                  <ns0:p n="27">27. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 34. 14.</ns0:note> Depart from evil, And do good <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Having therefore these glorious Promises and Priviledges, let no man do any Evil or unjust thing, to enrich or secure himself, nor abstaining from Pious and Charitable Actions, for f<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
